articles.summary: The vets say the mix-up occurred because they received two similar stray cats in quick succession.
articles.body:
A woman may have been given the wrong cat to bury due to a mix-up at the vets after it was run over.

Zoe Downs, from Seaham in County Durham, who had been feeding the stray animal for two years, took it to Seaham Vets and requested the body be returned to her if an owner could not be found.

But, after she had buried the animal, the vets called to say she may have been given the wrong cat, which she said left her "heartbroken".

Head vet Susan Turner apologised for Downs' distress. She said it was the practice's policy to not release the bodies of stray cats to members of the public in case the owner came forward but in this case an exception had been made as a "goodwill gesture".

Downs said she had been feeding the cat, which she named Bells, three times a day and took him to the vets after the accident on 13 October.

Turner said the mix-up had occurred because the team had received two dead stray cats within days of each other and both had been labelled "stray cat black and white" in cold storage.

On 21 October, Downs was given one of the body bags but Turner said she could not be sure if this was the correct cat as there were no other details on the labels.

Downs said the call from the vets to explain the possible mistake came about 15 minutes after she had buried the cat in her garden.

Downs said she and her husband had become attached to Bells over the past two years but accepted she was not his legal owner.

"He practically lived here and we bonded with him and we had toys outside for him and a little house for him to sleep in," she said.

"We wanted to put him to rest in a place that he loved.

Downs asked to be given the body of the second stray cat so it too could be buried in her garden but Seaham Vets refused.

Turner said nothing like this had happened at the practice before because of the usual policy of not handing over dead animals to anyone but the owner.

"If an owner then comes forward later, whether that cat's still in our care or not, the buck stops with us," she said.

Turner said the team acknowledged the mistake and measures had been put in place to ensure it did not happen again.

articles.title: Somerset cider makers warn rising costs risk traditional orchards
articles.summary: Producers claimed without more support, they could be forced to stop using British-grown apples.
articles.body:
Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses.

Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset.

The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers.

Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs.

Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider.

No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says

"By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed.

She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it.

"We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020."

"The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said.

"That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards".

Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole."

He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage.

"Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. "

The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations.

"Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said.

"We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing."

While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention.

"We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible."

Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings.

Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs.

"We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county."

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks.

"But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."

articles.title: Pectus excavatum: 'My deformity left me feeling invisible'
articles.summary: Charlie Clarke says the physical and emotional effects of pectus excavatum have been "unimaginable".
articles.body:
As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.

At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.

Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.

As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable".

"Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.

Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts".

"I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.

The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.

Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.

Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.

The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".

But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.

It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits".

If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.

But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.

Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety".

"It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."

That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.

A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.

Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.

What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17.

"I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said.

"It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied.

"It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."

McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.

"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said.

"If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services.

"But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."

McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.

Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.

She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister.

"I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.

Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.

A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.

It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.

One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.

It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.

Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.

In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".

It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery".

"The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."

Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.

Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term.

"If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."

articles.title: Land near Anglesey Abbey back with National Trust after 60 years
articles.summary: The trust hopes to restore the site, create new wildlife habitats and improve access to green space.
articles.body:
A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.

The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.

The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.

Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."

The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.

Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".

There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.

The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."

The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.

Community drop-in sessions about the vision will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.

Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

articles.title: Hundreds object to huge batteries on Wiltshire Rivals estate
articles.summary: The country estate where the batteries would be stored also hosts world music festival WOMAD.
articles.body:
Hundreds of objections have been lodged against proposals for a large battery storage facility on a country estate used to film hit TV drama Rivals.

Renewable energy company Grenergy wants to build a 450MW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) on land at Neston Park Estate, near Corsham, Wiltshire, which is also home to Peter Gabriel's WOMAD festival.

Concerns from locals over the 216 battery containers include fire safety and water contamination.

Grenergy said it takes safety "extremely seriously" and has a strategy to handle potential fires, adding water issues can be safely managed.

Closure of 114-year-old tearooms 'unfortunate'

Gritters out for the first time this autumn

No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says

The scheme would operate for 35 years, with Grenergy arguing battery storage is essential to store surplus renewable electricity and release it when demand is high - something the company said will play a "fundamental role in energy transition".

Wiltshire Council has yet to decide on the planning application.

Joe Exon, who lives 700 metres away from where the battery storage would be, is part of the campaign group against it - STOP Neston Bess.

He said: "The main concern is the sheer scale of this and why put it in this location.

"It's a historic location and its a substantial industrialisation of agricultural land.

"We're not a bunch of nimbys. We all know that we need to be improving our energy supply across the country. We need to be moving to renewables but this site doesn't actually generate any power at all."

Local councillor Vic Steadman said people see "no public benefit for it but a lot of social harm and harm to the environment, harm to ecology" as well as potential safety dangers after fires at similar sites.

The company said it will continue to "work closely with the communities to ensure they are informed as the scheme progresses through to operation".

It said the project's aim is to create a "positive impact".

There are concerns around fire safety linked to large lithium-ion battery installations

Grenergy said it has worked with the local fire and rescue service, who are satisfied with the proposals.

The strategy at the site would be to let one unit burn while dousing nearby ones with water so it does not spread.

There are concerns from locals that firewater would be contaminated with the chemicals from batteries, which would be at risk of reaching groundwater.

In a comment on the planning application, Wessex Water explained it is a "source protection area".

Grenergy said areas occupied by batteries would have impermeable membranes beneath them, and there would be a lined basin for contaminated water.

Another issue is noise - a specialist review commissioned by Neston residents challenged the applicant's assessment that there would just be low-frequency noise.

Grenergy said any risks can be safely managed, and that the proposed battery containers would use a more stable technology than some alternative battery storage methods.

articles.title: Loganair exploring operating routes to and from Guernsey
articles.summary: Loganair boss  Luke Farajallah says "we come in peace" as he visits the island for talks.
articles.body:
Loganair is exploring opportunities to operate routes from Guernsey, the airline's CEO has said.

Luke Farajallah said he was visiting the island for discussions about future aviation links, nearly a year on from when its licence applications to fly from the island - in the wake of the collapse of Blue Islands - were not approved by Guernsey's authorities .

He said: "We're not a hostile intruder, we come in peace."

Nico Bezuidenhout, CEO of States-owned airline Aurigny, said he thought "the jury is out to see what level of additional competition [the market] can sustain".

Loganair previously applied for licences to operate flights between Guernsey and Jersey and Guernsey and Southampton following Blue Islands' collapse, but withdrew its applications after they were provisionally refused.

Farajallah said any future expansion would need to be commercially viable and complement Aurigny and "if there's a match, then we will be there in a heartbeat".

He said: "I'd love to see Loganair's tartan tails across the whole of the UK and the Channel Islands, that's the right approach.

"I think consolidation in the market is inevitable where you have players of scale.

"They generally do dominate these sorts of islands' communities, and it's really important we give all island communities those options."

When asked what routes the airline were interested in operating, Farajallah added: "The key licence routes out of Guernsey are the ones that really do make Guernsey work and anything more than that may be based on a charter operation in the summer.

"Maybe some summer seasonal routes... we operate Bordeaux, we operate Paris and it's really easy to see how some of these connections could be made from Guernsey as well."

Aurigny's chief executive, Nico Bezuidenhout, said the island's aviation market was open to additional airlines, provided their services were complementary to existing connections.

He said of the market: "I think the jury is out to see what level of additional competition it can sustain."

Bezuidenhout said regardless of passenger demand "our reason for existence and our mandate from our shareholder is to protect lifeline routes".

He said of Aurigny's responsibilities: "We have to be there, I have to provide you six flights a day into Gatwick, whether there are passengers or not."

Farajallah said Loganair was not currently seeking to compete with Aurigny on the Guernsey-Jersey route, adding he did not see the need for two airlines operating the route.

articles.title: Plea for Haughley vets to keep animal mural painted in 1985
articles.summary: The owners of the vet surgery say they will be covering up the artwork but it will be preserved.
articles.body:
A former vet surgery worker has called on bosses to keep a 40-year-old animal mural that she says is part of the site's history.

The operator of the Haughley Veterinary Centre says artist Reg Siger's mural, painted in 1985 on the waiting room wall, will not be destroyed, but will be covered up.

Anita Burrell, who had worked at the surgery for 30 years, said the mural was "recognised by everyone locally" and called for a change of heart.

A spokesperson for Inspiring Vet Care, which runs the practice, said: "We fully appreciate the history and sentimental value of the mural and want to reassure everyone that it is not being destroyed."

Burrell said the mural was well loved locally.

"It's a comfort to those that are coming in to say goodbye and also a comfort to those that are bringing in kittens and puppies, to start on their relationships together," she said.

Siger, from Gislingham in Suffolk, said he was "a bit sad" to see it go, but the decision was "entirely up to the owners".

The subject matter was different to the artist, who normally paints buildings in Suffolk.

"I enjoyed doing it, it was a one-off. I haven't painted animals since," he said.

The artist said the idea behind the work was to make a place that can "sometimes be quite sad a little happier".

"Sometimes I use the vets to take the cat for a booster injection and I forget that I had done the mural. I see it and it brings a smile to my face," Siger said.

The vet's spokesperson said: "We're refreshing the practice to create a more welcoming environment for our clients and their pets.

"The mural will remain in place, carefully protected behind new panelling, and we will have it professionally photographed so that its story can be displayed in a prominent part of the practice.

"We're proud of the practice's history and are committed to respecting it as we make these improvements."

articles.title: In 2022, a Kerala woman cleared IELTS and mortgaged her property for a promised UK job; consultancy retained Rs 18.89 lakh from a Rs 20 lakh loan despite failing to arrange visa; consumer panel orders Rs 19.49 lakh refund
articles.summary: KOCHI: A woman in Kerala who mortgaged her property to finance a promised job in the UK was left without employment and facing loan liabilities after an
articles.body: KOCHI: A woman in Kerala who mortgaged her property to finance a promised job in the UK was left without employment and facing loan liabilities after an overseas recruitment consultancy allegedly failed to deliver on its assurance. The Pathanamthitta District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed the consultancy firm and its associates to pay her Rs 19.49 lakh, including Rs 18.89 lakh retained from a loan raised against her property, Rs 50,000 in compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The woman, a divorcee raising two children, had approached the consultancy in 2022 after completing a healthcare assistant course and clearing the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) examination. She was looking for an opportunity to work in the UK. The consultancy agreed to arrange a job visa for Rs 13.50 lakh. When she told its representatives that she could not afford the amount, they allegedly suggested raising the money through a chitty loan from the Kerala State Financial Enterprises (KSFE).Under the arrangement, she was asked to mortgage her property against a chitty scheme registered in the name of one of the consultancy's associates. She was assured that the loan instalments would be paid only after she found employment abroad.Trusting the promise, she handed over her property documents. The consultancy subsequently arranged a loan of Rs 20 lakh against her property, although the agreed cost of securing the UK job visa was Rs 13.50 lakh. The woman had initially paid the firm Rs 2.50 lakh on May 31, 2023, and received an offer letter. The amount was later returned after the loan was secured. The consultancy also paid Rs 10,266 towards an outstanding loan she had with another bank and gave her Rs 1 lakh for her children's education.However, she questioned why a loan of Rs 20 lakh had been raised when the agreed amount was considerably lower. She alleged that the consultancy failed to arrange the promised visa and stopped responding to her calls. When she visited its office, she learnt that several other people had also allegedly faced similar problems.She subsequently approached the consumer commission, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practices. In its October 15 order, the commission noted that none of the consultancy's representatives appeared before it.The panel noted that the woman had approached the consultancy after seeing an advertisement on Facebook in 2022. The firm provided assistance to people seeking employment overseas and operated through several associates and employees. The commission also recorded that the woman had lodged a police complaint against the consultancy's representatives. They subsequently agreed to release her property documents after clearing the outstanding liabilities.However, the consultancy defaulted on the chitty loan repayments. KSFE issued a registered notice to both the firm and the woman, asking them to clear the dues under the scheme registered in the firm's name. The panel found that the woman had received only Rs 1.10 lakh from the loan arrangement, including the amount provided for her children's education. The remaining Rs 18.89 lakh was retained by the consultancy and its associates. The commission directed the firm and the other opposite parties to refund Rs 18.89 lakh to the woman within 30 days. articles.title: Senedd presiding officer bans smart glasses from Welsh Parliament
articles.summary: The decision comes while a review of the use of the devices in the Senedd takes place.
articles.body:
The Senedd's presiding officer has in effect banned the use of smart glasses in the Welsh Parliament, days after it emerged he would allow them to be used as a teleprompter.

Huw Irranca-Davies had ruled that using them in such a way was OK - provided he was alerted first - but Members of the Senedd (MS) have now been told he "will not be considering any other requests" to use the devices.

Reform's Jason O'Connell made headlines earlier this year after using the glasses to help him make a speech .

O'Connell, whose glasses do not include a camera, said he had voluntarily agreed not to use his device until a review into using them on the Senedd estate ends.

O'Connell previously said he had started using glasses as a teleprompter to improve his speaking skills and to avoid looking down at his notes.

A letter from Irranca-Davies from 20 October, published in committee papers last week, said he had "determined that members may use smart glasses as a teleprompter in the chamber, provided that they give me advance notice".

On Tuesday, an official working for the presiding officer told MSs that "he will not be considering any other requests to use AI-equipped glasses in the Siambr until the review has reported".

They said: "Following further helpful discussions, no members will be using the technology until the review has been completed."

The official said the next stage of the Senedd Commission's review would include a consultation with MSs and staff, and would be completed by the end of 2026 with recommendations "brought forward in the new year".

O'Connell told BBC Wales after the decision: "I've voluntarily agreed to stop using the ones I'm using as a teleprompter until the review completes."

Asked how he felt about the matter, he said: "I'm ambivalent. They were a useful tool to be used on occasions.

"I was no way reliant on their use. But I look forward to using them again once the Senedd approves them."

The Senedd declined to elaborate on the statement to MSs after being asked why the presiding officer's stance had changed.

Reform is currently holding an unrelated boycott of Senedd proceedings , after its member Joe Martin was barred from speaking by Irranca-Davies, after Martin claimed in parliament that white people were being "replaced" in the UK.

The smart glasses decision was issued to MSs before the presiding officer's ruling on Martin was issued .

articles.title: DJ Zedd bought a Hollywood Hills home for $3.9 million in 2014 and listed it for $5.5 million in 2025; it has now sold for $4.25 million to fans who plan to turn his recording studio into a cinema
articles.summary: Grammy-winning DJ and producer Zedd has offloaded his Hollywood Hills home for $4.25 million, according to a report by Mansion Global.
articles.body: Grammy-winning DJ and producer Zedd has offloaded his Hollywood Hills home for $4.25 million, according to a report by Mansion Global. The four-bedroom house was listed for $5.5 million in 2025. The 1950-built home changed hands on Tuesday in an off-market deal. The local couple plans to transform Zedd’s recording studio into a cinema, agents Brandon Meneses of the Beverly Hills Estates and Janelle Meneses of The Agency, who represented the buyers, confirmed. “They’ve been looking for a long time and ultimately felt this was the right home for them,” Brandon told the outlet. The studio also played a part. According to the agent, the buyers are big fans of Zedd, and the recording space helped tip their decision. They plan to convert it into a cinema, so the room that once made music will now screen films.Inside Zedd’s former Hollywood Hills homeThe house is a modernist build dating from 1950, with 3,381 square feet of living space on just over a third of an acre. It sits at the top of a private driveway in Outpost Estates, behind a gate and a wall of greenery. The house has four bedrooms and six bathrooms. The renovation retained its modernist bones but made the rooms feel warmer. Wide white oak planks run throughout the home, and natural light comes in from almost every direction. The great room is the centre of it all. Folding glass walls on both sides open the space to city lights out front and the pool out back. Each of the four bedrooms has its own bathroom and access to a patio or balcony, while the primary suite’s balcony overlooks downtown. Outside, three fire pits, two at the front and one beside the heated saltwater pool, make the property usable year-round. Inside, a den has a wet bar and a built-in screening room with its own sound system. Carrara marble lines the walls, there’s a wine cellar, and an eight-camera security system can be monitored remotely. The house had been in Zedd’s ownership for more than a decade.Zedd bought the house in 2014 via a trust for $3.9 million, following the success of his debut studio album, ‘Clarity’, according to records from PropertyShark. The home went on the market in October 2025, with an asking price of about $5.5 million. It subsequently underwent several price cuts before disappearing from the market in early October. At that point, the asking price stood at $4.499 million, according to listing records.Zedd’s former Encino home was listed for nearly $18 million last month, according to Robb Report. He had previously purchased the property from Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner before selling it to pop star Meghan Trainor.In 2023, Zedd bought a Nordic-inspired mansion in LA’s Encino for $18.4 million. The house, named Odin, has roughly 18,000 square feet of living space, eight bedrooms, a guesthouse, a theatre, a wine cellar, a bowling alley, a wellness centre and a Junior Olympic-size pool.One of the richest DJs in the world, Zedd has an estimated net worth of $60 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth. articles.title: On Minnesota’s I-35W bridge, road sensors and a weather system detected conditions that could lead to ice, then triggered spray heads to distribute potassium acetate across the deck; an evaluation reported 68% fewer non-dry winter crashes
articles.summary: Discover how an innovative smart anti-icing system on Minnesota's I-35W bridge has reduced winter crashes by 68%. Learn about the technology and its environmental benefits in enhancing road safety.
articles.body: A bridge in Minnesota shows how technology can help prevent icy driving conditions before roads become unsafe. A smart anti-icing system installed on Interstate 35W in Minneapolis releases a chemical agent across the bridge before temperatures drop and ice forms. The system was made to prevent ice rather than simply clean it.An operational evaluation by the Minnesota Department of Transportation found that the method prevented 68% of non-dry crashes during evaluation, demonstrating the promise of automated road treatments to enhance winter driving safety. The system was installed on the I-35W bridge over the Mississippi River, where freezing conditions presented frequent challenges to travellers. Its proximity, heavy use, and exposure to the elements made the bridge especially susceptible to black ice, a transparent, smooth sheet of ice that often goes unnoticed by drivers.Why the I-35W bridge was vulnerable to winter accidentsThe I-35W bridge was chosen for this effort because of its record of winter crashes. A July 2001 operational evaluation reported that the bridge carried about 139,000 vehicles a day in 2000. Situated over the Mississippi River, the area was also exposed to moisture from industrial plants at Saint Anthony Falls and passing cars, creating conditions that could lead to ice formation.So drivers might have found themselves driving on slippery roads, potentially losing control of their vehicle more often than they anticipated, particularly during slower rush hours or periods of frequent congestion. To help combat this, road salt like sodium chloride was already being used for winter road maintenance. And now the bridge needed to be equipped with a system that could detect the onset of these potentially hazardous situations as soon as possible and treat them effectively.How the automated anti-icing technology worksThe system takes information from two kinds of pavement sensors to gauge conditions where ice might form. These consist of temperature and moisture sensors. In addition, the system includes ice-detection sensors and a road weather information system that measures temperature and rain, sleet, and snow. This information is communicated to a computer system at MnDOT’s dispatch centre approximately five miles from the bridge. When the combined readings suggest danger is imminent, the computer initiates the appropriate spraying program. Leaks are then checked before the spray equipment is powered up.Flashing yellow warning lights at the intersection advise motorists that the system is active. The system is made up of 38-valve units linked to 76 spray nozzles on the bridge deck. Potassium acetate is sprayed from each nozzle in a fan-shaped pattern to disseminate the liquid across the whole width of the highway. Rather than dispensing the entire supply at once, the computer releases the solution in sections based on readings. The actual spraying cycle takes 10 to 12 minutes, with each nozzle transmitting the solution for just over 2 seconds.Potassium acetate was chosen as a de-icer because it is effective at low temperatures and is much less damaging to the structure and reinforcing steel than typical chloride-based de-icers. It is environmentally friendly and contains no chloride, which is found in typical road salt. Furthermore, the research published in Accident Analysis and Prevention examined how ice detection sensors could help transportation agencies monitor road conditions, improve driver awareness, and support automated anti-icing systems.The 68% reduction in crashes and its wider implicationsThe performance of the installation was also evaluated during two winter seasons of operational testing. The evaluation examined results from the 2000 to 2001 winter season and compared them with the results from the 1996 to 1997 winter season. The latter was selected because the weather conditions were similar to those in 2000 and 2001. The analysis indicated that non-dry crashes were reduced to 31 in comparison to 10 in the test winter. This indicated that the 68% reduction in non-dry winter crashes occurred.The assessment also disclosed a benefit-to-cost ratio of 3.4, signifying that the projected benefit will surpass the cost of installation, upkeep, and chemical supply. The initial installation cost was about $578,365, and the adjusted final cost was $618,450.10. Further testing revealed problems with upkeep, as a few spray nozzles clogged with solid ice and snow during ploughing, and the chemical also sprayed in excess onto the bridge deck. This indicates that routine maintenance and correct positioning of the spray were necessary.The system’s environmental advantages also require careful consideration, although potassium acetate does not add chloride. Research published by the University of Minnesota found that too high a concentration could be harmful to aquatic life, suggesting the chemical should be used selectively rather than broadly. Thus, the I-35W project ultimately showed how monitoring the weather using pavement sensors and automating the application of chemicals can work to avoid the winter road black ice problem. Its results also provided transportation agencies with an example of how to use technology to improve safety at bridges where standard winter maintenance is difficult.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Hopeful they will come': India on inviting Pakistan to SCO Civilisational Forum in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has invited Pakistan to the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi from November 20
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has invited Pakistan to the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, with Union culture minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat saying he remained hopeful that Islamabad would participate."I should be hopeful that they will come," Shekhawat said at a press conference while discussing the invitations sent to participating countries.Prime Minister Narendra Modi will attend the inauguration of the forum on November 20, Shekhawat said.According to the minister, India sent invitations to 25 countries, including SCO member states, and 15 have confirmed their participation so far. China, Iran and Kazakhstan are among the countries that have confirmed their presence.The forum will be held at Purana Qila in Delhi and is intended to strengthen cultural understanding and people-to-people ties among SCO member states.Shekhawat said the grouping should serve as more than a geopolitical platform and also provide a space for countries to discuss their shared civilisational heritage.Unesco sites, shared heritage on agendaThe minister said discussions at the forum would include multinational nominations for Unesco sites. The initiative is also expected to promote cultural cooperation and a better understanding of the region's shared heritage.The proposal for the civilisational dialogue forum was put forward by PM Modi during his visit to Tianjin for the SCO summit last year. The initiative was aimed at fostering closer people-to-people connections and cultural understanding within the grouping.India's invitation to Pakistan comes despite strained bilateral ties. Pakistan's minister for national heritage and culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, was invited to the meeting.The SCO has continued to provide a platform for engagement between the two countries even in the absence of substantive bilateral talks.Pakistan's then foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto visited India in 2023 for an SCO foreign ministers' meeting, while external affairs minister S Jaishankar travelled to Pakistan in 2024 for a meeting of the grouping's heads of government. Neither visit resulted in a bilateral meeting.India to host inaugural editionIndia's decision to host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum was announced by defence minister Rajnath Singh at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, last month.Singh had invited all SCO member countries to participate in the initiative, which is intended to strengthen cultural ties and mutual understanding.He had also referred to the need for closer cooperation among member states on security, connectivity and regional opportunities, while stressing a collective approach to tackling terrorism.The forum in Delhi will be the inaugural edition of the initiative.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Two street vendors identified as victims of the L.A. metro station crash
articles.summary: Authorities have identified two of the three women killed when the driver of a minivan crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station this week.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Authorities have identified two of the three women killed when the driver of a minivan crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station this week. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner identified the women as Teodora Villalobos, 57, and Maria Peck, 73. Both were killed on the sidewalk Tuesday by blunt force injuries, the medical examiner’s office said. Authorities did not immediately release the identity of the third victim, pending the notification of family, the medical examiner’s office said in an email on Thursday. Peck and Villalobos were food vendors in Los Angeles’ North Hollywood neighborhood who were killed when the minivan plowed into a busy intersection during the height of the evening commute. Friends and family members built a memorial to the women, who were widely known for selling hot dogs and other street food, by leaving flower bouquets, notes, photos and candles on the sidewalk where they were struck. Police arrested the driver, 61-year-old Ihor Demianenko, for investigation of driving under the influence and three counts of murder. His bail was set at $6 million. It was not immediately known when he would appear in court. Melissa Villalobos told KABC-TV that her mother worked hard and tried to help those in her community. “When she sold here, if people didn’t have money to pay for the food, she would still give food to those who didn’t have anything,” she said. Peck worked as a vendor for more than a decade six days a week, even on holidays, according to a GoFundMe page set up to support her family. The page said Peck found joy in being part of the community and didn’t want to scale back her hours even as she aged.

articles.title: On Montana’s State Route 200, crews applied 3,000 gallons of magnesium chloride during and after a storm; the treated Plains section was bare afterwards and had a 37% lower four-year average cost per lane-mile than Thompson Falls
articles.summary: Discover how Montana's strategic use of magnesium chloride on State Route 200 during winter storms resulted in clearer roads and significant cost savings compared to traditional methods.
articles.body: Picture two stretches of the same highway after a winter storm. One is clear and dry, while the other is covered with packed snow and ice. According to the Federal Highway Administration case study, ‘Montana DOT Anti-Icing/Deicing Operations,’ a winter storm threatened State Route 200 in Montana on 14 December 2000. In the Plains section, crews applied 3,000 gallons (about 11,355 litres) of magnesium chloride during and after the storm. The result was a bare pavement.Two roads, one stormTwo teams looked after the route. The Missoula maintenance division was responsible for Plains, while the Kalispell division was responsible for Thompson Falls. Both areas experienced different weather conditions. Plains received just 8 inches (20 cm) of snow. Thompson Falls, on the other hand, received 15 inches (38 cm) of snow followed by eight hours of freezing rain. Both places were about the same temperature.The two crews also chose different techniques. At Thompson Falls, 800 gallons of chemicals were used to pre-wet abrasives, which were then spread on the packed snow. An additional 750 gallons of magnesium chloride was used for anti-icing and de-icing in an area that didn't meet air quality standards. After the storm had passed, the road was covered by compacted snow and ice. Drivers complained about the sharp change where the two sections met.What the cost figures showed To understand the difference, the Montana Department of Transportation’s Maintenance Review Section interviewed managers and reviewed material used and operating costs from 1997 to 2000. These figures cover those four years, not the single storm. Plains had a four-year average of $1,095 per lane-mile annually. Thompson Falls had a four-year average of $1,750. A lane-mile is one mile of a single lane. That made Plains’ approach 37% cheaper. The savings were found in a variety of places. Labour cost 52% less. The cost of equipment was 44% lower. Sand was 44% cheaper, and crews used 41% less of it. Plains did spend more on magnesium chloride, $233 per lane-mile compared with $136. But it had a lower overall bill. The case study noted that Plains achieved a higher level of service with safety and mobility benefits, and fewer abrasives benefited the environment. Thompson Falls did face the heavier storm that day, but the cost averages span four winters.Acting early made the difference The review cited timing as a crucial factor here. Treatment with anti-icing products before or just as the storm started kept snow from compacting or made it easier to clear off. A later reaction required several rounds of material. It also offered only a temporary grip on snow-covered roads. This was the review’s general finding on preventive versus reactive treatment; the case study says only that Plains’ 3,000 gallons went on during and after the storm.Management practices were equally important. Plains managers ordered chemicals on the basis of an average winter and allowed the field supervisors to order additional amounts. By contrast, the managers of Kalispell estimated the requirement at the beginning of winter and bought no extra amount. Thus, Plains had a salt content of 7.5% in the sand mix, while Thompson Falls had 4%. Following the review, Kalispell raised its salt share from 4 to 7%.The limits of chemicals Magnesium chloride is not a cure-all for freezes. Researchers at Montana State University, writing in a 2025 report for the Montana Department of Transportation, put its working limit at -12°C, against about -9.4°C for common salt. They add that salt can accelerate the corrosion of steel in concrete bridges. The same report looks back at the Plains case. The researchers explain that the results show the cost-effectiveness of preventive treatment over reactive treatment. In their own work, they examine geothermal heat for bridge decks, tapping warmth from the ground. Lab tests and simulations suggested the system kept a bridge surface above freezing at -10°C with 10°C fluids entering the pipes. It's a feasibility study, so it does not prove the idea works on real bridges yet.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Families across 43 US states were offered rent-to-own plans advertised as 90-day deals but allegedly faced costs near twice the cash price; a proposed $183.5 million settlement would provide refunds and debt relief
articles.summary: Families across 43 US states could receive refunds and debt relief under a proposed $183.5 million settlement with rent-to-own finance company Acima
articles.body: Families across 43 US states could receive refunds and debt relief under a proposed $183.5 million settlement with rent-to-own finance company Acima Digital, following allegations that the company misled customers about payment plans advertised as 90-day deals. According to Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday's November 12 announcement, the multistate agreement resolves allegations that consumers were automatically enrolled in rental-purchase agreements lasting up to 12 months, potentially leaving them paying nearly twice the original cash price of furniture, electronics and other merchandise. The settlement includes $43 million in consumer refunds, $130 million in lease balance reductions and $10.5 million for participating states.The agreement involves Acima Digital LLC and its parent company, Acima Holdings LLC. The company partners with retailers to offer customers rent-to-own arrangements, allowing them to obtain merchandise immediately and make payments over an agreed period. Such arrangements are often marketed as an alternative for people who may struggle to qualify for traditional credit or financing.However, attorneys general from 43 states alleged that Acima's advertising and enrolment practices gave customers an incomplete picture of what they were signing up for. The company allegedly promoted its rental-purchase agreements as 90-day payoff programmes without clearly explaining that customers could be automatically placed into agreements with a maximum term of 12 months.How the 90-day offers allegedly turned into year-long paymentsAccording to the allegations outlined by Pennsylvania and Ohio attorneys general, customers were attracted by advertisements suggesting they could pay off their merchandise within 90 days. However, the states claimed that Acima did not adequately disclose that consumers were automatically enrolled in longer rental-purchase agreements. Under these arrangements, customers could end up paying approximately twice the cash price advertised by the retailer if they continued with the full 12-month payment schedule.The states also alleged that Acima used terms such as "credit" in marketing its products, leading some consumers to believe they were signing up for conventional financing rather than a rental-purchase agreement. The distinction is significant because rent-to-own arrangements operate differently from traditional loans, with customers generally making payments to rent merchandise and having the option to acquire ownership under the agreement's terms.The investigation also raised concerns about how customers were presented with contracts. Attorneys general alleged that the company's electronic signing process obscured important terms and conditions, making it difficult for consumers to understand the full cost and duration of their agreements before accepting them.Another allegation concerned the process of ending these arrangements. The states claimed that Acima made it difficult for customers to terminate their agreements by returning merchandise, potentially leaving them with financial obligations they had expected to avoid. The coalition further alleged that the company marked up the cash prices of merchandise above the prices charged by its retail partners, adding to the amount consumers could ultimately pay.A $183.5 million settlement to help consumersThe proposed agreement divides the financial relief into three major components. According to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office, $43 million will be distributed as consumer restitution, $130 million will go towards reducing outstanding lease balances and $10.5 million will be paid to participating states.The Ohio Attorney General's Office provided a breakdown of the expected relief for residents in that state. Ohio consumers are expected to receive nearly $5 million in lease forgiveness across more than 4,000 agreements, while over $900,000 in restitution will be distributed among more than 3,000 customers.Pennsylvania, meanwhile, expects more than $1.6 million in consumer restitution and approximately $3.6 million in lease forgiveness. The state's attorney general said almost 9,000 Pennsylvania consumers could benefit from the settlement through refunds, paid-off leases or forgiven balances.Eligible consumers will not need to submit an application immediately to be considered for relief. Those entitled to restitution will be contacted by the settlement administrator, while customers eligible for lease forgiveness will be contacted directly by Acima. Further instructions will be provided to affected consumers.Company must change advertising and payment practicesBeyond financial compensation, the agreement requires Acima to make changes to how it advertises and administers its rental-purchase agreements. The company must ensure that important information about payment periods, costs and contract conditions is clearly disclosed in its advertisements. It must also make the terms of agreements more visible during electronic signing, rather than presenting customers with processes that could obscure important details.Acima will also be required to stop marking up the cash prices charged by its retail partners and cannot obstruct customers from ending agreements by returning merchandise. The settlement additionally requires the company to train its retail partners so they can explain the arrangements more accurately.Another significant condition concerns credit reporting. Acima has agreed not to report these rental-purchase agreements to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, the three major US credit reporting agencies, for five years. The company must also properly address issues involving delayed deliveries, damaged merchandise and repairs where required by the agreement or state law.The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau had previously raised concerns about Acima's business model. In an amended complaint filed in September 2024, the agency alleged that the company's virtual rent-to-own arrangements could cost consumers more than twice the original retail price and that its enrolment and contract practices harmed customers. Those earlier allegations provide additional regulatory context to the latest multistate action.Acima's parent company, Upbound Group, said in a November 12 statement that the agreement resolves a multistate investigation dating back to 2021. The company said the settlement does not include findings or admissions of wrongdoing and that the payment had already been reserved in its 2025 financial statements.The consent petition has been filed in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas in Pennsylvania and is awaiting judicial approval. Until the court approves it, the proposed settlement is not final.For families affected by the alleged practices, the agreement could mean more than refunds. It could also eliminate outstanding lease balances and introduce changes intended to make the true cost of rent-to-own arrangements clearer before customers commit to them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amritpal Singh gets 1-day interim bail to attend grandmother's last rites
articles.summary: AMRITSAR: A local court has granted one-day interim bail to Khadoor Sahib MP Amritpal Singh on Saturday to attend the cremation of his grandmother, Charan
articles.body: AMRITSAR: A local court has granted one-day interim bail to Khadoor Sahib MP Amritpal Singh on Saturday to attend the cremation of his grandmother, Charan Kaur.Shamsher Singh Padhri, chief spokesperson of Amritpal Singh-led Akali Dal Waris Punjab De (ADWPD), told the media that the MP had been granted one-day bail, while his uncle, Harjeet Singh, and another relative, Sukhman Singh, had been granted three and two days' bail, respectively. He said it was not yet clear when Amritpal would arrive in Amritsar or which flight he would take.The family had earlier deferred Charan Kaur's cremation by three days, urging the government to grant the jailed MP parole so that he could attend her last rites. Her mortal remains have been kept at the family's native village, Jallupur Khera, in Amritsar.Akali Dal Waris Punjab De leader Manpreet Singh Ayali had also demanded parole for Amritpal, saying that Sikh political prisoners were being denied basic humanitarian relief even as people accused of heinous crimes were repeatedly granted parole."Bhai Amritpal Singh's grandmother, Mata Charan Kaur, has passed away, and her family has postponed the cremation in the hope that he might be allowed one last glimpse of her," Ayali, the Dakha MLA, had said."This is a simple appeal for natural justice as per the norms of a civilised society. A grandson's right to bid farewell to his grandmother cannot be selectively denied. Authorities must rise above double standards and grant him temporary parole without delay," he had said.The family had also approached a court in Amritsar seeking Amritpal's temporary release.Amritpal, founder of Akali Dal Waris Punjab De, is lodged in a jail in Assam in connection with the 2023 Ajnala police station attack case.On February 23, 2023, Amritpal and his supporters, some of whom were allegedly carrying swords and firearms, barged into the Ajnala police station on the outskirts of Amritsar and clashed with police while attempting to secure the release of his aides detained there.He was arrested in Moga's Rode village on April 23, 2023, following a month-long manhunt. articles.summary: Microsoft's global outage continued to disrupt businesses and government operations across several countries on Friday, with banking services affected in
articles.body: Microsoft's global outage continued to disrupt businesses and government operations across several countries on Friday, with banking services affected in Hong Kong, government systems facing problems in Australia and Japan, and courts reporting delays in the Philippines. The disruption, which began on Thursday, has left millions of users struggling to access essential services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams and other Microsoft 365 applications.More than 12 hours after the US technology giant first reported the issue, its engineers were still struggling to restore services fully. Microsoft reported some progress but acknowledged that attempts to improve serviceability were not working as expected. The company said it had found no evidence of malicious activity behind the disruption.Here are the top developments from the global Microsoft outage:Hong Kong banking services disrupted: Employees at major financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, reported disruptions to their work after being unable to access emails and Microsoft Teams. Speaking to CNN, one banker said some emails were arriving sporadically, but millions of messages were potentially stuck in a backlog. The disruption also affected businesses relying on communications with overseas customers. Australian government services, schools affected: Schools, courts and government services in Australia experienced disruptions as employees struggled to access Outlook and other Microsoft applications. Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft had compared the incident to the CrowdStrike outage of July 2024. Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator. Microsoft did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack and suspected an update-related problem, he said.Japan turns to physical documents: The outage affected government IT infrastructure in Japan, with ministries and agencies struggling to send emails through much of Friday's working day. Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said government employees were responding by making physical copies of documents. He added that authorities were closely monitoring developments.Philippine courts report delays: The Supreme Court of the Philippines said the Microsoft 365 disruption had affected some of its operations. In a post on X, it warned that responses to emails and other transactions could be delayed while the disruption continued.Singapore government emails affected: Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it was working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.Indian airlines report email disruptions: IndiGo said the outage had affected its email support services, limiting its ability to receive customer queries. However, its other customer support channels remained operational and flight operations were unaffected. Akasa Air issued an advisory informing passengers about delays in its email support services.US businesses face disruption: Several US city governments reported widespread email problems and advised residents to contact local offices by phone where necessary. Industrial technology company Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings conference call because of the disruption.AI platforms report connectivity issues: OpenAI and Anthropic also reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, highlighting the wider impact of the outage on platforms that rely on integrations with other companies' software.What we know about the Microsoft outageMicrosoft said the disruption was affecting a broad range of Microsoft 365 services that interact with its Exchange Online and email infrastructure. Outlook, Teams and its AI assistant Copilot were among the services users reported having trouble accessing.The company said it was taking a measured approach to identifying and repairing the affected infrastructure while exploring different ways to determine the cause of the problem and restore services.The outage spread rapidly, with tracking website Downdetector recording disruptions across 74 countries and territories within roughly an hour. More than 130,000 users reported problems accessing Outlook at the peak of the disruption on Thursday.Microsoft initially reported that it had made progress in restoring service health and functionality. However, a subsequent update indicated that the changes were not delivering the expected results."We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected," Microsoft said in an update on X.The company said it was identifying alternative workstreams to address the disruption and would continue treating the incident with urgency until services were fully restored.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Bond denied for South Carolina man accused of burying his 11-month-old son alive
articles.summary: A South Carolina man accused of burying his 11-month-old son in a dog crate in a clump of scrubby pines was denied bond.
articles.body: LEXINGTON, S.C. — A South Carolina man accused of burying his 11-month-old son in a dog crate in a clump of scrubby pines was denied bond Thursday. Michael Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder, burglary and unlawfully placing a child at risk in connection with the disappearance of Koah Sharp, who survived and is expected to make a full recovery. Tyler Douglas, lead investigator for the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, told Magistrate Gary W. Reinhart on Thursday morning that Comer showed no remorse for attempting to kill his son and tried to flee the state. Reinhart subsequently approved a public defender for Comer and set a hearing for Dec. 10. Comer has been in custody in Lexington County since Monday, when his son was reported missing. An attorney has not yet been appointed for him. Koah, who rescuers found after about 24 hours, was released from a hospital Tuesday night, Sheriff Jay Koon said. John Comer said he’d opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay. He showed an Associated Press reporter the small hole on a neighbor’s property where rescuers uncovered the child. “God had to have laid in the ground with Koah for the entire, entirety of that time,” he said after Thursday’s bond hearing. “Only God can deliver miracles in this fashion.” Authorities haven’t revealed anything about Comer’s motive. He was sentenced in October to probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence involving the boy’s mother. Court records show that in May he pushed her from behind while she was holding Koah, causing the baby to hit a clothes dryer. Koah’s parents “have had some situations,” the sheriff said. “Children,” he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle.” Family members have identified the mother as Dezarae Sharp. The AP could not locate a phone number for her, and she has not responded to messages sent to her social media accounts. In a 911 call released Thursday, Patricia Comer told a dispatcher that her son had “severe schizophrenia and bipolar and depression.” She said she had been “kindly worried” about leaving Koah with his father that morning. “He threatened to kill himself last night and asked me for some sleeping pills,” she told the dispatcher. “He kept making comments that he was going to take (unintelligible) to New York, which he cannot, because he’s on probation.” But John Comer said his son, from whom he has been largely estranged, seemed perfectly rational when he picked him and Koah up and took them to his home. He said his son told him he had a job and a plan to care for Koah. “He was not emotional,” John Comer said outside the law enforcement complex Thursday. “He was not excited. He was just, he appeared a loving, a loving and caring father. He fed the baby. He changed the baby’s diaper. He held the baby. The baby played for a while. He was in his right mind.” Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside for the boy. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below, the sheriff said. Koah likely survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel that was wrapped around the crate below ground, he said. John Comer said the crate was “just a piece of junk” he had lying around his house. He said he has no “sympathy or pity” for his son, and shudders to think what might have happened had he not picked them up that day. “Koah’s alive,” he said, choking back a sob. “He’s alive. That’s what matters.”

articles.title: Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why?
articles.summary: Outlook, Teams and Copilot remain disrupted in 74 countries as Microsoft reports ‘marginal success’ in fixing outage.
articles.body:
Microsoft says it has had only “marginal success” in restoring its most widely used workplace services, more than 12 hours after a global outage knocked out Outlook and disrupted Teams and Copilot for users in 74 countries.

In a statement on its service health page early on Friday, the company said it was monitoring activity across regions to assess server status and find ways to improve capacity. “This includes reviewing server performance and confirming that developed patches have been applied and working as intended after infrastructure reboots are completed,” it said.

Here is what we know about the outage, what caused it and when services might return.

Problems with Microsoft products began at about 16:00 GMT on Thursday, when users began reporting that they could not access Outlook, its email platform. Within about an hour, the outage tracker Downdetector had logged reports from 74 countries and territories.

Microsoft first said it was investigating problems in the Americas, but later confirmed that users in any region could be affected. It said the affected infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which was likely contributing to the connectivity errors.

The company later said a number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, and that the elevated load had not been caused by an increase in traffic.

The disruption dragged on through the US working day and into the night. By Friday morning in Europe, it had still not been resolved, and servers Microsoft had restored were failing again.

“I don’t think it’s unprecedented. I mean, the scale is impressive,” Rupert Goodwins, a technology analyst and journalist, told Al Jazeera “It’s very embarrassing for Microsoft and really, really annoying for the rest of us.”

Microsoft has not confirmed the number of users who have been affected.

Data from Downdetector, through which users can report problems with online services, gives a partial picture, however.

At about 07:00 GMT on Friday, it had received at least 43,000 reports of problems with Outlook from users in 72 countries. The true number is likely far higher, since the figure only counts people who visit the site to report an issue.

“There’s about 430 million people who use Microsoft services,” said Walter Pasquarelli, an affiliate researcher at the Bennett School of Public Policy at the University of Cambridge and an AI specialist. “What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk.”

Government systems in Singapore and Japan have been disrupted, as have communications at the Supreme Court of the Philippines. In Australia, the country’s spy agency and federal police were among the organisations hit.

Which Microsoft services have been affected?

Outlook has been hit hardest. Users have reported being unable to open their mailboxes via the web, the app or through mobile devices, and many emails which do go through have arrived late.

Other services have been partly disrupted. The disruption has spread beyond Microsoft’s own products, hitting integrations which other companies, including the AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic, rely on.

“For the most part, we don’t really think about it too much, a little bit like our health, that we kind of take these tools for granted until they’re suddenly down or they’re not there,” Pasquarelli said.

What caused the Microsoft outage? Was it a cyberattack?

Microsoft has not published a root cause but said the outage was not the result of a cyberattack.

On Friday, it was rolling back a network change, but did not say if that change was to blame for the problems.

“We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said in a post on X late on Thursday.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft had also told him it did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack. “They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told a news conference in Sydney.

Goodwins said elevated load usually comes from one of two places. “Either there’s an external attack and some aggressor is trying to put lots and lots of artificial loads on the system to break it,” he said. “Microsoft says that hasn’t happened, and I believe them because there are ways to mitigate that.”

The other common cause, he said, is a faulty update to internal systems. “The update gets sent out over the administration network to all these servers, but there’s a mistake, and instead of it fixing things, it makes them reset or stop being able to talk to each other,” he said.

Pasquarelli said the evidence so far points to a technical failure. “It could literally be like a cable that basically damaged some of the infrastructure. It could be a sign of basically incompetence. It could be a mistake on some of their automated systems,” he said. “So far I do not see any evidence that points to an extremely high amount of computational power or traffic that is caused by AI systems.”

Goodwins said Microsoft’s focus on AI may have played an indirect role. “Microsoft has been completely focused on AI, and I imagine that the stuff like email and Teams, they’re just seen as forgotten revenue source. They won’t have got the investment and thought and management mind space they should have done,” he said.

“It does also show that for all Microsoft’s AI, it hasn’t got any AI that can help fix the networks,” he said.

Why are Microsoft’s efforts to fix it not working?

Microsoft has posted a series of updates on X about the progress it is making to restore service. Late on Thursday, it reported only limited recovery as it tried to route users’ traffic away from affected servers, and later said the changes it had applied were not taking effect as expected.

“Some of these servers basically started failing some automated health checks, and then the traffic would go to some of the other servers, and they would then get overloaded,” Pasquarelli said.

“Think of it a bit like a highway where you have four lanes, and now all of a sudden you have two lanes. That means that there’s a lot more traffic, and because there’s traffic, then the entire thing shuts down,” he said.

Goodwins said servers knocked offline usually attempt to reconnect so they can synchronise their files again. “As things come back up, they’re immediately swamped by the traffic from all the other servers desperate to talk to them. So it all falls down again,” he said.

“When the traffic accident’s cleared, there’s gridlock. There’s a huge backlog of traffic, and the roads can’t cope with it,” he said.

Goodwins also said many experienced engineers have left Microsoft. “It’s not so much that there aren’t enough human eyes, but all the experienced people, the people who built the stuff up, have left,” he said. “There’s been a draining of corporate memory of how these systems are built up and how they work.”

When will Outlook, Teams and Copilot be restored?

Microsoft has not given a timeline for full recovery. It has said that as capacity returns, users may see service come back gradually as their apps reconnect, rather than all at once.

“It’s fairly early on in the story. We don’t know all the facts,” Goodwins said. “It’s been going for a long time, and Microsoft’s been quite open in the fact the fixes aren’t really working yet.”

What can users do while Microsoft services are down?

There is little users can do themselves, as the problem lies with Microsoft’s servers rather than their own devices. The desktop version of Outlook may still show emails already downloaded, while Teams chats and calls have largely continued working.

Goodwins said the short-term impact of such outages tends to be limited. “You can’t log on to your email for a bit. Well, that happens all the time because your broadband’s down or your local computers stop working,” he said. “It comes back up and you grumble a bit and get back on with life.”

Pasquarelli said organisations should plan for such disruptions. “What is the minimum viable service or the minimum viable product that we need to keep up if there’s a global outage?” he said.

How does this compare with previous outages?

This is not Microsoft’s first major outage this year. In January, Microsoft 365 went down across North America for almost 10 hours. The company blamed that on heavy service load combined with reduced capacity during maintenance.

In late August, thousands of Outlook users worldwide were locked out of their mailboxes.

Other tech companies have suffered similar failures. In October 2025, an Amazon Web Services outage took down a large number of websites and apps.

In July 2024, a faulty software update from the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike crashed computers around the world, cancelling flights, disrupting hospitals and causing billions of dollars in losses.

The outage comes as Europe pushes for greater technological sovereignty, aiming to run its own servers and depend less on foreign providers. Lacking tech giants of its own, the continent relies heavily on US firms for digital services.

That push has gained momentum during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as he has imposed tariffs on Europe and threatened to take over Greenland, a Danish territory.

Earlier this year, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said government officials would stop using Zoom and other US-owned video conferencing tools in favour of French software, partly to reduce “dependencies on non-European actors”.

“With the whole thing about digital sovereignty, meaning that you can’t trust that your data is secure if it’s being served by an American company because of changes to US legislation, certainly in Europe, there have been big pushes to find alternatives to Microsoft, and this sort of thing will only increase the pressure,” Goodwins said.

He added that Microsoft has relied on “intensive inertia”. “People feel they have to stick with Microsoft because the pain of transitioning somewhere else is too great. But at some point, that pain threshold changes,” he said.

Goodwins said he did not expect an immediate impact on Microsoft’s revenue, because customers are tied into licensing contracts. “I think in the long term it probably will, but in the short term, and it’s quarter-by-quarter business here, it won’t,” he said.

Pasquarelli said he could envisage a short dip in Microsoft’s shares, but that its dominance of office software would be hard to replicate. “I don’t think that there’s any firm, at least not in Europe, that because of this outage could provide a credible and solid alternative,” he said. He added that organisations are more likely to “focus more on their digital resilience instead of building something of their own”.
